blocks.p: So they went on, and Ignorance followed. They walked until they came to a place where another road joined their own and seemed to run just as straight as the one they ought to take; and here they did not know which of the two to follow, for both seemed to lie straight ahead of them. So they stood still to consider. And as they were thinking it over, a man came up to them, dark and foul of body but covered with a robe of shining white, and asked them why they were standing there. They told him they were going to the Celestial City but did not know which of these roads to take.
“Follow me,” said the man. “That is where I am going.”

So they followed him down the road that had just come into theirs. Little by little it turned, and turned them so far from the city they wanted to reach that before long their faces were set away from it; and still they followed him. Then, before they knew it, he led them both inside the reach of a net, and they were so tangled in it that they did not know what to do. With that, the white robe fell from the man’s back, and they saw the darkness beneath it, and saw where they were. There they lay for some time, crying, for they could not get themselves out.

“Now I see my mistake,” said Christian to his companion. “Didn’t the Shepherds tell us to beware of the Flatterer? What the wise man said, we have found true today: ‘A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.’” [Prov. 29:5]

“They also gave us a note of directions for the way, so that we could be surer of finding it,” said Hopeful, “but we forgot to read that too, and so we have not kept ourselves out of the paths of the destroyer. David was wiser than we were. He says, ‘As for the deeds of men, by the word of your lips I have kept myself from the paths of the destroyer.’” [Ps. 17:4]

So they lay in the net, lamenting. At last they saw a Shining One coming toward them with a whip of small cords in his hand. When he reached them, he asked where they had come from and what they were doing there. They told him they were poor pilgrims on their way to Zion, but had been led out of their way by a dark figure dressed in white, “who told us to follow him,” they said, “because he was going there too.”

“It is Flatterer,” said the one with the whip, “a false apostle who has disguised himself as an angel of light.” [Prov. 29:5; Dan. 11:32; 2 Cor. 11:13-14] He tore the net open and let the men out. “Follow me,” he said, “so that I can set you on your way again.” And he led them back to the road they had left to follow the Flatterer.
Then he asked them, “Where did you spend last night?”
“With the Shepherds, on the Delectable Mountains.”
“Didn’t those Shepherds give you a note of directions for the way?”
“Yes.”
“Then when you came to a stand, did you take out your note and read it?”
“No.”
“Why not?”
“We forgot.”
“And didn’t the Shepherds tell you to beware of the Flatterer?”
“Yes,” they said, “but we never imagined that this fine-spoken man was he.” [Rom. 16:18]

Then I saw in my dream that he commanded them to lie down; and when they did, he whipped them hard, to teach them the good way in which they should walk [Deut. 25:2]; and as he whipped them he said, “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline. So be earnest, and repent.” [2 Chron. 6:26-27; Rev. 3:19] When this was done, he told them to go on their way and pay close attention to the Shepherds’ other directions. So they thanked him for all his kindness and went quietly along the right road, singing:

v: Come here, all you who walk along the way,
and see how pilgrims fare who go astray:
they’re caught and tangled in a net, and why?
Because they let good counsel pass them by.
It’s true they were set free; and yet, you see,
they’re whipped as well. Let this your warning be.

blocks.p: Now after a while they saw someone far off, coming quietly and alone along the highway to meet them.
“Over there is a man with his back toward Zion,” said Christian, “and he is coming to meet us.”
“I see him,” said Hopeful. “Let’s be on our guard this time, in case he turns out to be a flatterer too.”
So the man drew nearer and nearer, and at last came up to them. His name was Atheist, and he asked them where they were going.
“We are going to Mount Zion,” said Christian.
At this Atheist burst into loud laughter.
“What do you mean by laughing?” asked Christian.
“I’m laughing at what ignorant people you are, to take on such a wearisome journey, when all you’re likely to get for your pains is the walk.”
“Why, man, do you think we won’t be received?”
“Received! There is no such place as you dream of in all this world.”
“But there is in the world to come.”

“When I was at home in my own country,” said Atheist, “I heard what you are saying now, and on the strength of it I went out to see. I have been looking for this city for twenty years, and I’ve found no more of it than I did the first day I set out.” [Jer. 22:12; Eccl. 10:15]
“We have both heard and believe that there is such a place to be found,” said Christian.

“If I hadn’t believed it when I was at home, I wouldn’t have come this far looking for it. But I’ve found nothing, and I should have, if there were any such place, for I’ve gone farther looking for it than you have. So I’m going back, and I’ll try to enjoy myself again with the things I threw away for the hope of what, I now see, does not exist.”
Then Christian said to Hopeful, “Is it true, what this man says?”

“Be careful,” said Hopeful. “He is one of the flatterers. Remember what it has already cost us once to listen to his kind. What! No Mount Zion? Didn’t we see the gate of the city from the Delectable Mountains? And aren’t we to walk by faith now? Let’s go on,” said Hopeful, “before the man with the whip catches up with us again. [2 Cor. 5:7] It’s you who should have taught me the lesson I’ll now ring in your ears: ‘Stop listening, my son, to instruction that leads you away from the words of knowledge.’ [Prov. 19:27] I tell you, my brother, stop listening to him, and let us be among those who ‘believe and are saved.’” [Heb. 10:39]

“My brother,” said Christian, “I didn’t ask because I doubted the truth of our faith myself, but to test you, and to draw out of you some proof of the honesty of your heart. As for this man, I know he has been blinded by the god of this world. Let you and me go on, knowing that we believe the truth, ‘and no lie comes from the truth.’” [1 John 2:21]
“Now I rejoice in the hope of the glory of God,” said Hopeful.
So they turned away from the man; and he, laughing at them, went his way.
I saw then in my dream that they went on until they came into a certain country whose air naturally made a stranger drowsy. Here Hopeful began to grow very dull and heavy with sleep.
“I’m getting so drowsy now that I can hardly keep my eyes open,” he said to Christian. “Let’s lie down here and take a nap.”
“By no means,” said Christian, “or we may sleep and never wake again.”
“Why, my brother? Sleep is sweet to the working man. A nap might refresh us.”

“Don’t you remember that one of the Shepherds told us to beware of the Enchanted Ground? He meant that we should beware of sleeping. ‘So then, let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober.’” [1 Thess. 5:6]

“I admit I was wrong,” said Hopeful. “If I had been here alone, I would have slept and run the risk of death. I see that the wise man was right when he said, ‘Two are better than one.’ Your company has been a mercy to me all this way, and you will have a good reward for your labor.” [Eccl. 9:9]
“Then,” said Christian, “to keep off drowsiness in this place, let’s fall into some good conversation.”
“With all my heart.”
“Where shall we begin?”
“Where God began with us. But you begin, if you will.”
“First I’ll sing you this song,” said Christian:

v: When saints grow sleepy, let them gather near
and listen to these pilgrims talking here;
yes, let them learn from them the way to keep
their heavy eyes from closing into sleep.
The fellowship of saints, if managed well,
will keep them wide awake, in spite of hell.

blocks.p: Then Christian began. “I’ll ask you a question. How did you first come to think of doing what you are doing now?”
“Do you mean, how did I first come to care about the good of my soul?”
“Yes, that’s what I mean.”
“For a long time I went on delighting in the things that were seen and sold at our fair; things that I now believe would have drowned me in ruin and destruction if I had kept on in them.”
“What things were they?”

“All the treasures and riches of the world. I also took great delight in carousing, wild parties, drinking, swearing, lying, impurity, breaking the Sabbath, and whatever else tends to destroy the soul. But at last, by hearing and thinking about the things of God, which I heard from you, and also from dear Faithful, who was put to death in Vanity Fair for his faith and his good life, I found that ‘the end of these things is death’ [Rom. 6:21-23], and that because of these things ‘the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience.’” [Eph. 5:6]
“And did you give in to this conviction right away?”
“No. I didn’t want to know the evil of sin right away, or the damnation that follows from committing it. When my mind first began to be shaken by the Word, I tried to shut my eyes against its light.”
“But why did you treat the first workings of God’s blessed Spirit in you that way?”

“There were four reasons. First, I didn’t know that this was God’s work in me. I never imagined that God begins the conversion of a sinner by awakening him to his sin. Second, sin was still very sweet to my flesh, and I was reluctant to leave it. Third, I couldn’t see how to part with my old companions; their company and their ways were so pleasant to me. Fourth, the hours when conviction was on me were so troubling and so frightening that I couldn’t bear even the memory of them.”
“So it seems that sometimes you got rid of your trouble.”
“Yes, I did. But it would come back into my mind, and then I’d be as bad as before, or worse.”
“Why, what brought your sins to mind again?”
“Many things,” said Hopeful. “For instance:
1. if I so much as met a good man in the street;
2. if I heard someone reading the Bible;
3. if my head began to ache;
4. if I was told that some of my neighbors were sick;
5. if I heard the bell toll for someone who had died;
6. if I thought about dying myself;
7. if I heard that sudden death had come to others;
8. but most of all, when I thought about myself, and that I must soon come to judgment.”
“And could you ever shake off the guilt of sin easily, when it came on you in any of these ways?”
“No, not I. Then it took a firmer hold on my conscience; and if I so much as thought of going back to sin, even though my mind was set against it, it was a double torment to me.”
“And what did you do then?”
“I thought I must try to mend my life; otherwise, I thought, I’m sure to be damned.”
“And did you try to mend it?”

“Yes. I ran not only from my sins but from sinful company too, and took up religious duties: prayer, reading, weeping over my sins, speaking the truth to my neighbors, and many other things, too many to tell.”
“And did you think you were well then?”
“Yes, for a while. But at last my trouble came tumbling back on me, right over the top of all my reforms.”
“How did that happen, now that you were reformed?”

“Several things brought it on, especially sayings like these: ‘All our righteous deeds are like filthy rags’ [Isa. 64:6]; ‘By the works of the law no one will be made right with God’ [Gal. 2:16]; ‘When you have done everything you were told to do, say, We are unworthy servants’ [Luke 17:10]; and many more like them. So I began to reason with myself: If ALL my righteous deeds are filthy rags; if NO one can be made right with God by keeping the law; and if, when we have done ALL, we are still unworthy, then it is foolish to think of reaching heaven by the law. And I thought further: If a man runs up a debt of a hundred pounds with a shopkeeper, and after that pays cash for everything he buys, still, if the old debt stands in the book uncrossed, the shopkeeper can sue him for it and throw him into prison until he pays.”
“Well, and how did you apply this to yourself?”

“I thought: By my sins I have run up a great debt in God’s book, and my reforming now will not pay off that account. So, for all my present improvements, I still had to ask: How shall I be freed from the damnation I have brought on myself by my past sins?”
“A very good application. But please go on.”

“Another thing that has troubled me, even since my reforms, is this: if I look closely at the best of what I do now, I still see sin, new sin, mixing itself in with the very best of it. So I am forced to conclude that, in spite of all my former fond opinions of myself and my duties, I have committed enough sin in a single duty to send me to hell, even if my former life had been faultless.”
“And what did you do then?”

“Do! I didn’t know what to do, until I opened my heart to Faithful, for he and I knew each other well. And he told me that unless I could obtain the righteousness of a man who had never sinned, neither my own righteousness nor all the righteousness in the world could save me.”
“And did you think he was telling the truth?”

“If he had told me that when I was pleased and satisfied with my own reforms, I’d have called him a fool for his trouble. But now that I saw my own weakness, and the sin that clings to my best efforts, I was forced to agree with him.”
“But when he first suggested it, did you think there was such a man to be found, of whom it could truly be said that he had never sinned?”
“I admit the words sounded strange at first; but after a little more talk and time with him, I was fully convinced.”
“And did you ask him who this man was, and how you could be made right with God through him?”

“Yes, and he told me it was the Lord Jesus, who sits at the right hand of the Most High. ‘And this is how you must be made right through him,’ he said: ‘by trusting in what he did himself in the days of his life on earth, and in what he suffered when he hung on the cross.’ I asked him further how one man’s righteousness could have the power to make another man right before God. And he told me that he was the mighty God, and that he did what he did, and died the death he died, not for himself but for me; and that all he did, and all its worth, would be counted as mine if I believed in him.” [Heb. 10; Rom. 6; Col. 1; 1 Pet. 1]
“And what did you do then?”
“I raised objections against believing, because I thought he was not willing to save me.”
“And what did Faithful say to that?”

“He told me to go to him and see. I said that would be presumption. But he said no, because I was invited to come. [Matt. 11:28] Then he gave me a book written by Jesus, to encourage me to come more freely; and he said of that book that every letter and stroke of it stood firmer than heaven and earth. [Matt. 24:35] Then I asked him what I must do when I came. He told me I must plead on my knees, with all my heart and soul, for the Father to reveal his Son to me. [Ps. 95:6; Dan. 6:10; Jer. 29:12-13] I asked him how I must make my plea, and he said, ‘Go, and you will find him on a mercy seat, where he sits all year round to give pardon and forgiveness to those who come.’ I told him I didn’t know what to say when I came. And he told me to say something like this: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner, and help me to know and believe in Jesus Christ; for I see that if his righteousness had not been, or if I do not have faith in that righteousness, I am utterly lost. Lord, I have heard that you are a merciful God, and that you have appointed your Son Jesus Christ to be the Savior of the world; and also that you are willing to give him to such a poor sinner as I am, and I am a sinner indeed. Lord, take this opportunity, then, and show the greatness of your grace in the salvation of my soul, through your Son Jesus Christ. Amen.’” [Exo. 25:22; Lev. 16:2; Num. 7:89; Heb. 4:16]
“And did you do as you were told?”
“Yes. Over, and over, and over.”
“And did the Father reveal his Son to you?”
“Not the first time, nor the second, nor the third, nor the fourth, nor the fifth; no, not the sixth time either.”
“What did you do then?”
“What! I didn’t know what to do.”
“Didn’t you think of giving up praying?”
“Yes, a hundred times, and a hundred more.”
“And why didn’t you?”

“I believed what I had been told: that without the righteousness of this Christ, the whole world could not save me. So I thought to myself, If I give up, I die; and I can only die at the throne of grace. And along with that, this came into my mind: ‘Though it delays, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not be late.’ [Hab. 2:3] So I kept on praying until the Father showed me his Son.”
“And how was he revealed to you?”

“I didn’t see him with my bodily eyes, but with the eyes of my understanding [Eph. 1:18-19]; and this is how it happened. One day I was very sad, sadder, I think, than at any other time in my life; and the sadness came from a fresh sight of how great and vile my sins were. And as I was expecting nothing but hell and the everlasting damnation of my soul, suddenly, as I thought, I saw the Lord Jesus Christ look down on me from heaven and say, ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved.’ [Acts 16:30-31]

“But I answered, ‘Lord, I am a great, a very great sinner.’ And he answered, ‘My grace is enough for you.’ [2 Cor. 12:9] Then I said, ‘But Lord, what is believing?’ And then I saw from that saying, ‘Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty,’ that believing and coming were one and the same; and that whoever came, that is, whoever ran after salvation by Christ with all his heart and longing, truly believed in Christ. [John 6:35] Then tears stood in my eyes, and I asked further, ‘But Lord, can such a great sinner as I am really be accepted by you and saved by you?’ And I heard him say, ‘Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.’ [John 6:37] Then I said, ‘But Lord, how must I think of you as I come to you, so that my faith rests on you rightly?’ And he said: ‘Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.’ [1 Tim. 1:15] ‘He is the end of the law, so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.’ [Rom. 10:4] ‘He died for our sins, and was raised again so that we might be made right with God.’ [Rom. 4:25] ‘He loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood.’ [Rev. 1:5] ‘He is the mediator between God and us.’ [1 Tim. 2:5] ‘He always lives to intercede for us.’ [Heb. 7:24-25] From all this I gathered that I must look for righteousness in his person, and for the payment of my sins in his blood; and that what he did in obeying his Father’s law, and in submitting to its penalty, was not for himself, but for anyone who will accept it for his salvation and be thankful. And now my heart was full of joy, my eyes full of tears, and my love was running over for the name, the people, and the ways of Jesus Christ.”
“This was truly a revelation of Christ to your soul. But tell me exactly what effect it had on your spirit.”

“It made me see that the whole world, for all its righteousness, stands condemned. It made me see that God the Father, though he is just, can justly declare righteous the sinner who comes to him. It made me deeply ashamed of the vileness of my former life, and overwhelmed me with a sense of my own ignorance; for never before had a thought come into my heart that showed me the beauty of Jesus Christ like this. It made me love a holy life, and long to do something for the honor and glory of the name of the Lord Jesus. Yes, I thought that if I had a thousand gallons of blood in my body, I could pour it all out for the sake of the Lord Jesus.”
